series.title: Arrival
series.blurb: Alex has a year in Japan on a working holiday visa. First, he has to get there.

chapters.title: I'm here
chapters.body:
来た。ついに来た！

日本…ついに、ついに来た！

meets.name: アレックス
meets.about: from Canada, in Japan for a year

chapters.title: Narita
chapters.body:
成田だ。日本だ！

大きい空港だ。

人、人、人だ。

chapters.title: Which way?
chapters.body:
人が多い！空港が大きい！

駅…あっち？あっちだ。

chapters.title: Out the window
chapters.body:
外は山だ。山、山、山。

大きい山だ。きれい！

日本は、きれいだ。

chapters.title: Tokyo
chapters.body:
東京だ！

人が多い。ビルが高い。ビル、ビル、ビル。

山は？あ、山はあっちだ。

高いビルが、きれいだ。
translations: Oh, the mountains are that way.

ここだ。大きいな。きれいだ。

grammar.title: ～た
grammar.summary: た on the end of a verb puts it in the past, the way friends say it: 来る (come), 来た (came).
grammar.body:
ついに来た！
お腹すいた。

notes.text: Verbs change their endings to say when, and whether, something happens. The plain past ends in た, or だ after some verbs.
This plain form is what you use with friends. The polite past, ～ました, comes later.

grammar.title: だ / です
grammar.summary: だ ends a sentence that says what something is: 成田だ, it's Narita. Friends say だ or leave it off; strangers and staff say です.
grammar.body:
成田だ。
いい部屋だ！

notes.text: だ comes at the very end of the sentence. In casual talk it's often left off, especially in questions.
です means the same thing, politely. You'll hear it from staff and strangers.

grammar.title: は
grammar.summary: は marks what you're talking about. It's written は but said "wa". On its own with a rising voice, it asks "what about…?"
translations: Where's the station? (What about the station?)

notes.text: The topic comes first, then は, then what you say about it.

grammar.title: が
grammar.summary: が points at who or what does something, or what a description is about: 人が多い, there are lots of people.
grammar.body:
人が多い。
ビルが高い。
translations: There are a lot of people.

notes.text: は sets the topic for what follows; が picks out the one thing the sentence is about. Often either works, with a slightly different feel.

grammar.title: ～ない
grammar.summary: ない on a verb makes it negative, the way friends say it: わかる (understand), わからない (don't understand).
grammar.body:
わからない。
いない。

notes.text: The verb's ending changes before ない. For る verbs, drop る: 食べる, 食べない. For others, the last sound moves to the "a" row: わかる, わからない.

grammar.title: よ / ね
grammar.summary: よ at the end tells someone something they don't know yet. ね looks for agreement, like "right?" or "huh".
grammar.body:
ユキだよ。
いい部屋だね。

notes.text: よ is friendly emphasis: you're filling the listener in.
ね assumes the listener sees it the same way.

grammar.title: の
grammar.summary: の joins two nouns, like 's or "of": アレックスの部屋, Alex's room.
grammar.body:
アレックスの部屋。
ここのラーメン。

notes.text: The first noun owns or describes the second.

grammar.title: ～たい
grammar.summary: たい on a verb's stem means you want to do it: 食べる, 食べたい, want to eat.

notes.text: Drop る from a る verb, or move other verbs to their "i" sound, and add たい: やる, やりたい.
It changes like an adjective: 食べたくない is "don't want to eat".

grammar.title: を
grammar.summary: を marks what a verb is done to: ラーメンを食べる, eat ramen. It's said "o".

notes.text: Friends often drop it: ラーメン、食べる？ means the same.

grammar.title: も
grammar.summary: も means "too" or "also", in place of は, が or を: これも, this too.
grammar.body:
ラーメンも食べたい。
これも！

grammar.title: です / ます
grammar.summary: Staff, strangers and bosses speak politely: verbs end in ます, and "is" is です. You'll hear it long before you need to say it.
grammar.body: 今日から、お願いします。

notes.text: ます goes on a verb's stem, the same stem as たい: 食べます, 飲みます. Its negative is ません, and its past is ました.
Friends would say the plain form instead. Using ます with friends sounds distant; leaving it off with strangers sounds rude.

grammar.title: ～てください
grammar.summary: A verb's て form plus ください politely asks someone to do something. Friends just use the て form.
grammar.body: ちょっと待ってください！

notes.text: The て form of 待つ is 待って. With friends, 待って on its own is enough.

grammar.title: に
grammar.summary: に marks where something goes, or where it is: 店に来た, came to the shop.

notes.text: It also marks times: 朝に, in the morning. In casual talk it's sometimes dropped after places.

grammar.title: ～てる / ～ている
grammar.summary: A verb's て form plus いる says something is going on now. Friends shorten ている to てる.

notes.text: It can also mean a state that's ongoing: 知ってる, I know (I'm in the state of having learned it).

grammar.title: から / まで
grammar.summary: から marks where or when something starts; まで, where or when it ends: 朝まで, until morning.

notes.text: They work with places and times, together or apart.
